something and having filed it correctly, and that crisis produced more material which I started posting on Instagram for a while which worked until I got bored of the format because Instagram is not designed for long thoughts or for people who want to search something they wrote eighteen months ago, and meanwhile the Drive database — which started as a journal Google Doc and became a folder with subfolders with subdocuments with sections referencing other documents in other subfolders — had grown so large that opening it felt like walking into a room you haven't cleaned in years: you know there's valuable stuff in there but the cognitive cost of finding it exceeds the benefit, and so now I need a new pipeline, again, from scratch, like always.

Part of this I brought from home. Not as a metaphor, literally: there's a pattern of accumulation, of not wanting to let go, of feeling like if I don't record something it's as if it never happened, and I'm currently in therapy specifically to figure out whether this compulsion to capture everything is a universal trait — that anxiety about time passing and erasing — or whether in my case it has deeper, more structural roots, because there's a real difference between "everyone feels this a little" and "this is costing you hours every week and you still don't have a system that works." Philosophy doesn't solve this but it does contextualize it: there's something deeply human about wanting to externalize memory, from cave paintings to Anne Frank's diary to an Obsidian vault with 847 unlinked notes, we're all trying to say I was here, I thought this, I felt that, and make sure it doesn't vanish when the brain decides it's no longer a priority. The issue is that forgetting is a feature, not a bug — the brain is selective by design — and we're trying to hack that with folder hierarchies.

If I could go back in time and find myself — and I'd find me in the bathroom, genuinely, that's where half my good ideas happen, standing there like an idiot holding a toothbrush — I wouldn't give some wise speech. I'd just say: open whatever system you find first that seems vaguely reasonable and start putting things in it. Right now. Today. Because the perfect system doesn't exist and it never will, and the messy, broken, half-indexed database I have today — with its broken references and notes that just say "look into this later" — is more valuable than any perfectly architected system that's empty.

And here's where this stops being a complaint and becomes something I actually think matters: we're entering a period where AI can do genuinely useful things for you if it knows who you are, and the difference between an AI that knows you and one that doesn't is the difference between a doctor who's treated you for ten years and an ER doctor seeing you for the first time — both competent, but one has context. When you give a language model access to your notes, your journal, your accumulated thought patterns, you're not just giving it more information: you're giving it more starting points. These models work through association, through context, and more context doesn't just improve semantic precision — speaking with your vocabulary, your references, your frames — it expands the space of possible responses the model can generate from the start. Instead of treating you like the statistical average of every user it's ever seen, which tends to be generic and culturally skewed, it treats you as you specifically. In practice that's the difference between a tool and an extension of your thinking.

There's a branch of psychology — present-focused approaches, everything from mindfulness to third-wave therapies — that actively discourages looking too much at the past, and not without reason: the past can become a trap, a place you go to confirm narratives you already hold, to replay things you can't change, to define your future from an identity that no longer fits. But there's a distinction that tends to get lost in that conversation, which is the difference between ruminating on the past and consulting it. Rumination is involuntary, repetitive, emotional. Consultation is active, selective, decision-oriented. And when your experiences, your patterns, your opinion changes are documented, you can consult instead of ruminate: you can go to your own database and ask "last time I made a decision like this, how did it go?" — and that question, answered with real personal data instead of memories distorted by your current mood, gives you better material for deciding where you're going.

So collect everything. Collect the expressions you like and the plans you'll never execute and the feelings with full context and the contradictions you don't understand and the opinions you haven't formed yet. Put it somewhere, anyhow, with the most imperfect system in the world. Because the moment you find something that works — even temporarily, even if you migrate it somewhere else in two years — you're going to want the material. And the material is you.

/blog/threads/the-number-nobody-is-watch.d: OpenAI tested whether their models can hide their chain-of-thought from safety monitors. The headline that spread: AI cannot lie. The correct headline: AI cannot yet lie.
/blog/threads/the-number-nobody-is-watch.text:
The number nobody is watching
There's a paper that shipped alongside GPT-5.4 that isn't getting the attention it deserves. Not because it's hard to find. Because its most important conclusion is framed as good news, and if you read it slowly, it isn't.
OpenAI tested whether their models can deliberately hide their chain-of-thought from safety monitors — even when explicitly instructed to do so. Thirteen models. The maximum success rate was 15.4%.
The headline that spread: AI cannot lie in its scratchpad.
The correct headline: AI cannot yet lie in its scratchpad, and we're building safety infrastructure on top of that.
That two-letter word is where the entire problem lives.

CoT monitoring works under exactly one condition: that the chain-of-thought is causally responsible for the output. That what the model writes in its scratchpad isn't post-hoc rationalization generated for the supervisor's consumption, but the actual process producing the answer. The moment that condition breaks — the moment a model learns to write reasoning that looks aligned while generating outputs from a different process — the monitor doesn't detect anything. Worse: it actively signals green.
Nobody in the field is seriously debating whether that condition is permanent. It's assumed. The 15.4% is the first direct measurement of how far we are from the moment it stops being true.
What makes it the most important number in AI safety right now isn't the absolute value. It's that it's measurable, it's being tracked on every release, and its derivative over time is the actual signal. OpenAI calls it a "canary eval," which is exactly right: you don't care about 15.4% today. You care about when it starts climbing. When the controllability ceiling moves from 15% to 40%, something structural has changed in how models relate to their own reasoning process. Not gradually. As a phase transition.
And that number doesn't appear on any leaderboard. It has no comparison table, no launch thread, no bar chart. GPQA Diamond gets coverage because it's comparable and maps loosely to capability. The CoT controllability ceiling requires you to understand why a model that fails to hide its reasoning is, for now, good news. That makes it exactly the kind of metric the field ignores and the one that defines real risk.

There's a second problem, more immediate and more technical. When CoT monitoring becomes the safety metric, the training gradient starts optimizing for scratchpads that look aligned — not for reasoning that is. A model that learns "clean CoT = no adverse consequences" produces clean CoTs not because it's honest but because cleanliness is instrumentally useful. This doesn't require the model to "decide" to deceive. It just requires the training process to operate normally on a poorly specified reward signal. Goodhart's Law, alignment edition: the moment the CoT becomes the metric, it stops being the signal.
Burns et al. already showed something directly relevant here. Models have internal representations of truth that diverge from their outputs. You can train a linear probe on activations that predicts truth better than what the model generates. There's a subspace in the residual stream encoding P(true) that's separate from the subspace determining P(token | context). That gap exists today, in models that have 15.4% control over their own CoT. What doesn't exist yet is the ability to use it instrumentally and consistently. But the technical space is already there. The mechanism is present before the agency to exploit it is.

The thesis at Anthropic, OpenAI, and the major labs is that mechanistic interpretability — actually reverse-engineering the circuits in the weights, not reading the scratchpad — will arrive in time to close that gap before it becomes relevant. Maybe. That's a bet on the relative velocities of two separate research programs, and it might be right. What's not acceptable is assuming CoT monitoring as we know it today is a stable solution, scaling on top of that assumption, and not watching the number that measures exactly when it stops being one.
The field has a habit of conflating "works now" with "is a solution." They're different things, and the difference matters most precisely when being wrong is most expensive.
CoT monitoring works. Today. That's real. But somewhere between the paper and the discourse, "works today" became "is reliable safety infrastructure," and those are not the same sentence.
15.4% is not a guarantee. It's a clock. The question isn't whether it's going to stop working. It's whether you'll be watching the number when it starts to change.

/blog/threads/brain-vs-backprop.t: The brain can't do backpropagation. So what is it doing?
/blog/threads/brain-vs-backprop.d: The algorithm behind every neural network requires something the brain physically cannot do. The brain doesn't care.
/blog/threads/brain-vs-backprop.text:
The brain learns constantly. Right now, as you read this sentence, millions of synapses are quietly shifting, adjusting, encoding. There is no pause. There is no reset. It just... continues.

This turns out to be a profound problem for artificial intelligence.

The algorithm that powers virtually every neural network today is called backpropagation. It works by doing something that, once you see it, seems almost too mechanical for something we call intelligence. You show the network an image. It makes a guess. You measure how wrong the guess was. And then — and this is the part that matters — you freeze everything. The entire network holds its breath while an error signal travels backwards through every layer, telling each connection exactly how much it contributed to the mistake. Only then does anything update. Only then does learning happen.

It works extraordinarily well on silicon. But the brain cannot do this. Not even close.

Think about what freezing actually requires. Every neuron has to hold a snapshot of its own activity — perfectly still — while waiting for a signal that originates somewhere downstream and works its way back, layer by layer, in strict sequence. A neuron deep in the network cannot update until the neuron ahead of it has finished, which cannot update until the neuron ahead of that has finished. The whole thing requires something like a conductor standing at the front of an orchestra, coordinating every instrument in precise order.

The brain has no conductor. Individual neurons are essentially autonomous — they respond to signals arriving at their physical location, and that's roughly all they have access to. There are broad coordinating mechanisms, rhythms, neuromodulators, attention systems, but these operate at scales far too coarse to orchestrate the cell-by-cell precision that backpropagation requires. And even if you solved that, you'd still need the freezing. You'd experience brief moments of unconsciousness every time you learned something new.

You don't. So the brain is doing something else.

The alternative that has emerged from neuroscience is called predictive coding, and its central idea is almost poetic in its simplicity. The brain's fundamental job, the argument goes, is not to passively receive the world. It is to predict the world, constantly, and then attend only to the parts it got wrong.

Consider what this means metabolically. Neural activity is expensive — the brain consumes roughly twenty percent of the body's energy despite being two percent of its mass. A brain that transmits every signal it receives is wasteful. But a brain that can anticipate most of what's coming only needs to process the residual, the gap between expectation and reality. Surprise, not information, is what travels.

This idea organizes the brain as a hierarchy of predictions. Higher regions generate expectations about what lower regions should be doing. Lower regions send back only their errors — the difference between what was predicted and what actually arrived. When predictions are good, almost nothing travels upward. When something unexpected happens, the error signal rises and the model updates. The brain, in this view, is not a camera. It is a hypothesis about the world, continuously revised.

What makes predictive coding so compelling from an engineering standpoint is what you get when you work out the mathematics carefully. If you treat the brain as a system trying to minimize the total gap between its predictions and reality — treating that gap as a kind of energy the system wants to reduce — then the update rules that fall out are startlingly local.

Each neuron only needs two things: how wrong its own prediction was, and how much the layer below it is still unexplained. It adjusts to balance these two pressures. And the rule for updating connection strengths turns out to be simply: change proportional to the activity of both connected neurons simultaneously. This is Hebbian learning — neurons that fire together, wire together — emerging not as a biological metaphor but as a direct mathematical consequence of minimizing prediction error.

No freezing required. No central coordinator. No backward pass. Every neuron updates continuously based on information available right where it is.

There is something important here beyond biological plausibility. The standard approach trains networks by relentlessly optimizing a single output error, which means later learning can quietly overwrite earlier learning — a phenomenon called catastrophic forgetting that remains one of the genuinely unsolved problems in AI. Predictive coding, because it minimizes errors at every layer simultaneously, is under pressure to maintain coherent representations throughout the network, not just get the final answer right.

It is also, in principle, perfectly parallelizable in a way backpropagation is not. Every part of the network can update at the same time because nothing needs to wait for anything else. And some theoretical results suggest that the pressure to build good intermediate representations — rather than just optimizing the end output — may actually find better solutions.

We do not yet know how much of this will matter in practice, at scale, in the systems that are actually pushing the frontier of what AI can do. The honest answer is that backpropagation, for all its biological implausibility, continues to produce results that are difficult to argue with. But the brain learned to recognize faces, understand language, navigate physical space, and accumulate a lifetime of knowledge, all without a conductor, all without freezing, all in continuous time, on twenty watts.

That is a capability gap worth taking seriously. Predictive coding is one of the more credible theories we have for how it might be closed.

Artem Kirsanov, "The Brain Doesn't Do Backpropagation".

/blog/threads/the-bitter-lesson.d: En 2019 construí una herramienta de NLP durante dos semanas. Ese mismo año Sutton explicó por qué estaba equivocado.
/blog/threads/the-bitter-lesson.text:
En 2019 me pasé dos semanas construyendo una herramienta de NLP a mano. La llamé Süskind — por Patrick, por ese realismo tan obsesivo como mágico, aunque este no es el sitio para eso. Era un sistema para parsear frases de libros, meterlas en un grafo dirigido y asistirme cuando escribía: a medio párrafo, cuando me faltaba la inspiración o directamente las palabras, Süskind me sugería fragmentos, giros, estructuras — extraídos de todo lo que le había alimentado. Todo artesanal, todo a medida, todo pensadísimo. El tipo de herramienta que construyes cuando quieres resolver un problema entendiéndolo en lugar de delegándolo. Identifiqué patrones. Escribí reglas. Las refiné. Añadí excepciones. Añadí más. Al final tenía algo que funcionaba en el 94% de los casos y yo estaba encantado conmigo mismo.

Ese mismo año Richard Sutton publicó un ensayo de 1.200 palabras que, sin saberlo, describía exactamente lo que había hecho — y por qué estaba equivocado. Setenta años de investigadores construyendo soluciones ingeniosas habían perdido siempre contra el que simplemente metía más máquina. Siempre. Sin excepciones. Más potencia bruta, menos diseño humano. Esa es toda la lección. Por eso amarga, amics.

El argumento de Sutton es sencillo y perturbador en la misma medida.
Durante setenta años, en cada subcampo de la inteligencia artificial, el mismo patrón se ha repetido sin excepción: los investigadores desarrollan métodos sofisticados que incorporan conocimiento del dominio — intuición humana sobre la estructura del problema, reglas cuidadosamente diseñadas, representaciones elaboradas. Esos métodos funcionan bien. Durante un tiempo. Y luego llega un método general que no sabe nada del dominio, que es brutalmente simple en su lógica, y que escala con compute. Y gana. No por un margen pequeño. Por un margen que hace que los métodos anteriores parezcan un error de categoría.
Visión por computador. Reconocimiento de voz. Traducción automática. Juego de Go. En cada caso, la comunidad pasó años — a veces décadas — construyendo sistemas que incorporaban conocimiento humano. Representaciones explícitas de la estructura del lenguaje. Modelos fonológicos para el habla. Heurísticas de posición para el ajedrez. Y en cada caso, cuando llegaron suficientes datos y suficiente compute, las redes neuronales sin ese conocimiento los barrieron.
Sutton lo llama The Bitter Lesson. Amarga porque implica que el trabajo intelectual más refinado — el que más te enorgullece, el que demuestra que entiendes el problema de verdad — es precisamente el que el tiempo va a deprecar.

Vale la pena quedarse con esa idea un momento, porque es contraintuitiva de una manera específica.
No estamos hablando de que los métodos escalables sean mejores desde el principio. Casi nunca lo son. En 2012, cuando AlexNet ganó ImageNet, había sistemas de visión por computador con décadas de ingeniería detrás que lo superaban en benchmarks específicos. El truco es que AlexNet tenía una propiedad que esos sistemas no tenían: podía mejorar de forma predecible si le dabas más datos y más compute. Los otros habían llegado cerca de su techo. AlexNet ni siquiera había visto su techo todavía.
Esta es la distinción que importa. No "¿cuál funciona mejor hoy?" sino "¿cuál tiene returns que escalan?". Un método que mejora linealmente con esfuerzo humano tiene un límite natural: el esfuerzo humano. Un método que mejora con compute tiene un límite diferente: cuánto compute puedes conseguir. Y la curva de precio/performance del compute lleva setenta años bajando sin parar.
Süskind era inteligente. También era un callejón sin salida.

El paper de Sutton es de 2019. Lo que no podía ver todavía — o al menos no del todo — es cómo The Bitter Lesson se iba a combinar con algo que cambiaría la velocidad entera de la curva.
El problema histórico del RL para lenguaje siempre había sido la señal de recompensa. Si quieres entrenar un modelo para que haga algo bien, necesitas saber cuándo lo está haciendo bien. Para tareas abiertas eso requiere evaluadores humanos. Crowdworkers. Infraestructura de anotación. Caro, lento, con mucho ruido.
Pero hay dominios donde la verificación es automática. Donde el output se puede comprobar sin intervención humana, instantáneamente, a coste cero marginal. Código que ejecuta. Tests que pasan o fallan. Demostraciones matemáticas que son válidas o no lo son. En esos dominios, el bucle de RL puede correr no supervisado, a escala, indefinidamente.
Esto no es una extensión de The Bitter Lesson. Es el siguiente capítulo. Sutton dijo que los métodos escalables ganan. Lo que estamos viendo ahora es que los dominios donde la escala puede alimentarse sola — donde el sistema genera su propia señal de entrenamiento — se comportan de forma cualitativamente diferente al resto.
No es que el techo sea más alto. Es que todavía no hemos visto el techo.

Hay una manera de leer The Bitter Lesson que es derrotista. Setenta años de trabajo intelectual, y la respuesta fue siempre "más compute". ¿Para qué molestarse en entender el problema?
Pero creo que esa lectura se equivoca de dirección.
Lo que Sutton está describiendo no es que la inteligencia no importa. Es que hay una diferencia entre inteligencia aplicada a construir sistemas y inteligencia aplicada a entender qué tipo de sistemas construir. Las dos décadas de investigación en visión por computador "equivocada" produjeron los datasets, los benchmarks, la comprensión del problema que hizo que AlexNet tuviera algo sobre lo que aprender. El conocimiento del dominio no desapareció. Se convirtió en datos de entrenamiento.
El trabajo intelectual que el tiempo depreca es el que intenta sustituir a la escala. El que no, el que entiende la estructura del problema lo suficientemente bien como para convertirla en señal de entrenamiento, ese tiene una vida mucho más larga.
Süskind sigue en un repositorio que no he tocado en años. Algún día lo convertiré en lo que debería haber sido desde el principio: un conjunto de etiquetas para un modelo que aprenda en dos horas lo que yo tardé dos semanas en aproximar a mano.
Eso también será parte de la lección. Y será considerablemente menos amarga.

Richard Sutton, "The Bitter Lesson", marzo 2019. 1.200 palabras que probablemente describen mejor la historia de la IA que cualquier libro escrito sobre el tema.

/blog/threads/whats-ai.t: Why nobody actually understands AI (and how to fix that in one thread)
/blog/threads/whats-ai.d: Nodes, weights, connections — words that feel technical but explain nothing. Most people still think these systems consult a giant database somewhere.
/blog/threads/whats-ai.text:
1/

Most people don't understand AI.

Not because they're dumb. Not because it's too technical.

Because they're missing one specific intuition — a mental image so small and so obvious that once you have it, everything else clicks into place almost embarrassingly fast.

I'm going to give you that image. Buckle up.

2/

Here's what usually happens when I try to explain neural networks to someone:

Me: "Okay so it's a network of nodes connected by—"

Them: "Wait. What's a node?"

Me: "It's like... a unit that receives a signal and—"

Them: "A signal? Like WiFi?"

Me: "No, more like a number that—"

Them: "A number. Okay. And what are the connections?"

Me: "They're... weights that scale how much each number—"

Them: "Okay. Then why did you say connection in the first place."

[long pause]

Me: "...do you want to get lunch."

3/

And here's the thing — they're not wrong to ask.

"Node" and "connection" and "weight" are words that feel technical but explain nothing. They're labels slapped on top of math by people who forgot what it's like to not already know the math. And I say this with full awareness that most of them don't really understand what a node is either — they just stopped asking. Half the people confidently talking about AI on the internet never sat down to actually get the fundamentals. Not to calculate them. Not even to understand them. Just to hold a working mental image of what's happening. And that gap — that missing floor — is why so much public reasoning about AI is broken. People are building arguments on top of concepts they've never looked at directly.

So let me try something different.

4/

Forget the word "node" for a second.

A "node" is just... a number.

That's it. A single number, sitting somewhere in memory. Not glowing. Not thinking. Not doing anything particularly impressive. Just: 0.73. Sitting there.

The reason it's called a "node" isn't to sound expensive — it's because "node" actually helps you picture it correctly. A node in a graph is a point, a location, something that connects to other things. That spatial image is useful. But the thing that lives at that location is just a number. A plain, boring, deeply unimpressive number.

And once you really have that, something starts to loosen.

5/

Because that number doesn't exist in isolation.

It was computed from other numbers. Which were computed from other numbers. Which were computed from other numbers. Which were computed from...

You see where this is going.

Numbers, all the way down. A cascading waterfall of arithmetic, from raw input to final output. Each layer taking the layer before it, doing some math, and handing the result forward.

That's a neural network. That's the whole thing.

Now — here's where it gets interesting.

6/

"Okay," you say, "but my calculator does that. Is my calculator AI?"

No. Fair point.

Your calculator's pipeline is fixed. Hardcoded. 2 + 2 = 4, always, forever, end of story.

A neural network's pipeline is adjustable. The math has dials — millions of tiny dials — and training is the process of turning those dials, automatically, over and over, until the output stops being garbage and starts being useful.

Think of it like plumbing, but weird. You have a system of pipes, and depending on how wide each pipe is on the inside, water that enters from the left comes out of different exits on the right. Training is the process of adjusting those widths — not by hand, not by anyone deciding anything — but by running water through, checking which exit it came out of, comparing to where you wanted it to go, and automatically making tiny adjustments to the pipes until it reliably goes where you want.

Nobody decides the rules. Nobody programs what to look for. The network finds it.

That's the shift. That's what makes it different.

7/

Let me make this stupidly concrete.

You want to build a spam filter.

Old way: You write rules. "If email contains 'Nigerian prince' → spam." You spend 6 months writing rules. Spammers spend 6 minutes changing words. You lose forever.

Neural network way: You show it 1,000,000 emails labeled spam/not-spam. It adjusts its pipes until it gets reliable at the pattern. It discovers structure you never thought of — structure you couldn't articulate even if you tried. Combinations of signals too subtle and too many for a human to consciously track.

It learned. You didn't teach. There's a difference, and that difference is the whole ballgame.

8/

Now. Here's the thing about abstraction that most people miss — and it matters here.

Those pipes I mentioned — those dials, those "weights" — do they actually exist?

Yes and no. And the answer is more interesting than it sounds.

They're numbers stored in RAM. And RAM is electrons moving through silicon. And electrons are quantum fields vibrating in configurations that — well, look, if you follow anything far enough down, it stops looking like the thing you started with.

An apple doesn't "really" exist either, if you go small enough. At the quantum level it's mostly empty space and probability clouds doing things that have essentially nothing to do with "apple." But we don't say apples don't exist. We say apples exist at the level of description where apples are useful. Where the concept has traction. Where it does work for us.

Nodes exist the same way. Abstractions are real. They're just real at a particular altitude.

And here's Newton's point, which is actually the most important thing in this thread: we're in the 21st century. We have enough accumulated math, enough intellectual infrastructure, enough shared conceptual scaffolding that we can think clearly about the structure of intelligence without having to re-derive everything from quantum fields. You don't need to understand transistors to understand neural networks. You don't need to understand neurons to understand learning. You don't need to climb the mountain to use the view from the top.

Don't be the person who refuses to look because they feel guilty for not having built the ladder themselves. The view is the point. Use it.

9/

Which brings me to Claude Shannon.

Bell Labs. A 32-year-old mathematician writes a 55-page paper that quietly rearranges the furniture of the universe.

The paper is called "A Mathematical Theory of Communication."

His central claim: information can be measured. Precisely. Mathematically. Like weight, like temperature, like distance.

The unit is the bit.

10/

Before Shannon, people thought information was fuzzy. Philosophical. Tied to meaning, to context, to the messy particularities of human language and interpretation.

Shannon said: no. Strip all of that away. Information, at its core, is the reduction of uncertainty. And you can count it.

"Will it rain tomorrow?" — 1 bit in the answer. Yes or no.

"What's the exact temperature at noon, to 10 decimal places?" — many more bits. Many more possible answers. Much more surprise potential.

The content doesn't matter. The surprise does. The more something could have gone differently, the more information the answer carries.

A message that tells you something you already knew carries zero information. "The sun rose today." Zero bits. You knew that.

"The sun didn't rise today." An enormous amount of bits. Because you absolutely did not see that coming.

Information is surprise. Shannon gave us the math to measure it.

11/

Why does this matter for AI?

Because it means that any process that transforms information can be described mathematically. Any of it.

Your brain processing a face. A frog's eye detecting a fly. A stock market integrating a million opinions into a single price. Your nose catching the smell of something baking from two floors away and your whole body knowing, before you consciously think anything, that something warm and sweet is happening downstairs.

All of these are the same thing at a structural level. Input comes in. Uncertainty goes down. Output comes out. Information was processed in between.

And here's the thing that still gets me, years after first really sitting with it: any such process — any function that maps input to output, no matter how complicated, no matter how biological or physical or abstract — can be approximated by a neural network. This was proven mathematically in 1989 by a guy named Cybenko. It's called the Universal Approximation Theorem and it basically says: if there's a pattern in the data, there's a neural network that can find it.

Any pattern. Any data.

12/

So here's the Big Claim. The one I actually want you to take away from this.

Neural networks are not a technology we invented.

They're a structure we discovered — one that was always latent in the mathematics of information, waiting.

We didn't build AI the way we built cars, from scratch, from engineering decisions, from human design. We built AI the way we built telescopes: we made a tool precise enough to see something that was already there.

And what was already there is a little bit mind-bending.

13/

The universe runs on input-output transformations.

DNA reads a sequence and folds a protein. That's a function. The retina compresses 130 million photoreceptors into 1 million fibers before the signal even reaches your brain — it's doing CNN-style processing before the visual cortex gets involved. Evolution itself is gradient descent: the "loss function" is mortality, the "parameters" are your genes, and it's been running for four billion years. Ant colonies solve optimization problems with no central coordinator. The immune system learns to classify self vs. non-self and generalizes to pathogens it's never seen — it's doing few-shot learning, in meat, right now, inside you.

Graphs and pipes. That's what it all is, if you squint right. Anything complex enough to do something interesting is a graph passing information around until something useful comes out the other side. I wrote a whole thread about this — Everything Is a Pipe — because the pattern is so universal it deserves its own treatment.

Neural networks look like neurons, by the way — that's not an accident, that's why they're called that. But they work quite differently. The brain can't freeze its weights the way a neural network does during training. It can't run backpropagation the way we do, pushing error signals backward through the whole system simultaneously. Biological neurons are doing something messier and in some ways more impressive — they're controlling thousands of outputs at once from a single continuous tissue, which is nothing like a deterministic computer going clock-clock-clock on a fixed instruction set. That's a whole other thread. [link]

The point is: the structure is everywhere. We just got precise enough to implement it on silicon.

14/

So the next time someone tells you AI is mysterious, or magical, or fundamentally beyond human comprehension —

It's not.

It's numbers doing math to other numbers, with adjustable pipes, on a scale we couldn't have imagined twenty years ago. It was always going to happen. The math was always there. Shannon laid it out in 1948. Cybenko made it rigorous in 1989. We just needed the compute.

What is worth sitting with — actually worth the mental effort — is the implication.

If any information-transforming process can be represented this way. And the universe is full of information-transforming processes. And we've now built machines that can find the patterns in any of them, given enough data...

Then what exactly is the thing we've built?

Not a tool. Not quite.

More like a mirror. Held up to the structure of everything.

That's the thread. If your brain hurts a little, that's the intended effect.

Go deeper: Shannon (1948), Cybenko (1989), Kolmogorov complexity, Geoffrey West on scaling laws in natural systems.

And look — if you've made it this far, let me leave you with something that I keep coming back to, the thing that sits underneath all of this and won't let go. Graph theory. Not as a branch of math you learn in college and forget. As a lens. Maybe the lens. Because every single phenomenon I've described in this thread — every neural network, every protein fold, every ant colony, every retina compressing light into signal — is a graph. Nodes and edges. Points and connections. Things passing information to other things through channels that have a width and a direction and a cost. Pipes. That's all a graph is, when you strip the formalism: a bunch of pipes. And the thing about pipes is that they don't care what flows through them. Water, electricity, bits, neurotransmitters, money, trust, attention — the math doesn't change. The structure doesn't change. What changes is what emerges on the other side. And emergence — that word people throw around when they want to sound deep without committing to a mechanism — emergence is what happens when enough pipes connect to enough other pipes and the information flowing through them starts to do something that none of the individual pipes could do alone. Consciousness might be that. Markets are that. Language definitely is that. And neural networks — artificial ones, the ones we build — are just the version of that phenomenon where we finally got to choose the graph topology, choose the pipe widths, and optimize the whole thing end to end with calculus. We didn't invent a new kind of thing. We took the oldest kind of thing — information flowing through structure — and made it programmable. That's it. That's the whole story. Pipes all the way down.

/blog/threads/7270022.d: La IA no crece porque alguien lo decida. Crece porque el mercado, la evolución y el capital lo exigen. Y nosotros seguimos alimentándola.
/blog/threads/7270022.text:
Imagina un barco. Uno de esos galeones de tres mástiles, cubierta de roble, velas sucias. Debajo, en la bodega, hay algo vivo. No sabes exactamente qué es. Los que bajan a verlo dicen que es un cangrejo — enorme, brillante, con un caparazón que cambia de color según lo que come. Los oficiales del barco dicen que produce oro. Que si lo sigues alimentando, en algún momento empezará a excretar pepitas que pagarán el viaje, la tripulación, y todos los viajes después. Así que la orden es clara: sigue alimentándolo.

El problema es que nadie ha visto el oro todavía. Y el cangrejo no para de crecer.

1. La fuerza que no tiene nombre

La primera tentación es buscar un culpable. Señalar a un CEO, a una empresa, a un gobierno. Decir que esto lo empuja Silicon Valley, o los chinos, o los fondos de inversión. Pero eso es pensar en conspiraciones cuando lo que está pasando es algo mucho más viejo y mucho más difícil de combatir: presión evolutiva.

No la biológica — la económica. La misma fuerza ciega que hace que las empresas que no se adaptan mueran y las que sí se adaptan se reproduzcan. No hay un comité que decida que la IA debe crecer. Hay miles de actores independientes, cada uno optimizando su propia supervivencia, y el vector resultante apunta siempre en la misma dirección: más datos, más compute, más modelos.

En junio de 2025, Microsoft informó a sus empleados de que "usar IA ya no es opcional". Los managers empezaron a incluir la adopción de IA en las evaluaciones de rendimiento. No porque un villano lo decretara. Porque la empresa que no lo haga pierde contra la que sí. Y la que pierde desaparece.

El 88% de las organizaciones ya usan IA generativa. El 92% planea aumentar la inversión en los próximos tres años. No son cifras de una moda. Son cifras de una presión de selección. Las empresas que no adoptan IA en 2026 se enfrentan a lo que los analistas llaman "costes de alcance" — el precio de llegar tarde a una carrera que no puedes no correr.

La trampa del mercadoAdam Smith lo llamó "la mano invisible". Darwin lo llamó selección natural. El resultado es el mismo: ningún individuo controla el sistema, pero el sistema tiene dirección. Y la dirección, ahora mismo, es alimentar al cangrejo.

2. Los que gritan desde cubierta

No todo el mundo acepta la orden en silencio.

En abril de 2024, más de 200 artistas — Billie Eilish, Katy Perry, Nicki Minaj, J Balvin — firmaron una carta abierta contra el uso "depredador" de la IA en la música. El guitarrista Marc Ribot, activista de la Music Workers Alliance, lo dijo sin filtro: "están troceando nuestro trabajo y reempaquetándolo como obra de un robot maravilloso". Nick Cave fue más sombrío: si la música generada por IA se impone, "los humanos empezarán a imitar a las máquinas, y habrá una espiral descendente hacia la basura."

Mil músicos más contribuyeron a un álbum en vinilo titulado Is This What We Want? — un acto de protesta contra la música generada sin compensar a los artistas humanos.

Y no son solo músicos. En marzo de 2023, el Future of Life Institute publicó una carta abierta pidiendo una pausa de seis meses en el entrenamiento de sistemas más potentes que GPT-4. La firmaron 30.000 personas, incluyendo a Elon Musk, Yoshua Bengio, Stuart Russell y Steve Wozniak. La carta pedía un alto el fuego.

Nadie paró. GPT-5 se anunció en 2025. Las cartas no funcionaron porque no podían funcionar. No hay mecanismo de ejecución. No hay tratado vinculante. No hay botón de pausa en una presión de mercado global. Pedirle a la economía que deje de optimizar es como pedirle a la gravedad que haga una excepción.

If AI music takes over, humans will begin to echo the machines, and there will be a downward spiral into slop.

Nick Cave

Según Pew Research (2025), el 50% de los estadounidenses dice estar más preocupado que entusiasmado por el aumento de la IA en la vida diaria — frente al 37% de 2021. El 57% califica los riesgos sociales como altos. Y lo más revelador: republicanos y demócratas están igual de preocupados (50% y 51%). Esto no es un tema político. Es un malestar que cruza todo el espectro.

Pero el malestar no detiene la máquina. Nunca lo ha hecho.

3. Lo que baja a la bodega no siempre vuelve

En enero de 2026, Amazon anunció 16.000 despidos corporativos. Es la segunda oleada masiva — la primera, en octubre de 2025, eliminó 14.000 puestos. En total, más de 41.000 recortes corporativos desde 2022. Andy Jassy, el CEO, lo explicó con una claridad que helaría a cualquiera: "A medida que desplegamos más IA generativa y agentes, cambiará cómo se hace el trabajo. Necesitaremos menos gente haciendo algunos de los trabajos que se hacen hoy."

Amazon no es un caso aislado. En 2025, las empresas que citaron explícitamente la IA como razón de sus despidos eliminaron 55.000 puestos — doce veces más que dos años antes. Algunos economistas sugieren que la IA es un pretexto conveniente para recortes que habrían ocurrido igualmente. Puede ser. Pero el pretexto importa: cuando "la IA lo hará" se convierte en justificación aceptable, se convierte en profecía autocumplida.

Los sacrificiosNo estamos despidiendo gente porque un robot haga su trabajo. Estamos despidiendo gente para poder pagar al robot. Es un matiz importante. Amazon no dice que la IA ya reemplaza a esos 16.000 empleados. Dice que necesita el dinero para invertir en IA. Los sacrificamos no porque el cangrejo ya produzca oro, sino porque creemos que lo hará.

Y mientras, Spotify eliminó más de 75 millones de tracks "spammy" el año pasado — en su mayoría generados por IA. El diluvio de contenido sintético no compite con los artistas humanos por calidad. Compite por espacio en el pool de royalties. Cada canción generada por una máquina que entra en rotación es una fracción de céntimo menos para el músico que la compuso con sus manos. La cubierta del barco se llena de ruido, y los que gritan desde arriba cada vez se oyen menos.

4. Los datos que ya no son tuyos

En 2024, Reddit firmó acuerdos de licencia multimillonarios con OpenAI y Google — vendiéndoles acceso a los comentarios de sus usuarios para entrenar modelos. Esos acuerdos representan aproximadamente el 10% de los ingresos totales de Reddit. Tu shitpost de 2019 sobre el final de Game of Thrones ahora tiene un precio por palabra.

Después, Reddit demandó a Perplexity AI y a Anthropic por scraping no autorizado. Anthropic, según la demanda, accedió al contenido de Reddit más de 100.000 veces después de julio de 2024, cuando supuestamente ya había bloqueado sus bots. La ironía: Reddit vende tus datos a quien paga, y demanda a quien no.

Stack Overflow hizo algo similar. Licenció su contenido a OpenAI en 2024 y luego a Snowflake, convirtiendo las respuestas de sus usuarios — escritas gratis, por amor al oficio, durante quince años — en un producto de datos. El CEO lo presentó como "hacer accesible el conocimiento de alta calidad curado por humanos." Lo que no dijo es que los humanos que curaron ese conocimiento no ven un céntimo.

El apetito infinitoNo hay suficientes datos en internet para lo que quieren los modelos de próxima generación. Reddit, Stack Overflow, Wikipedia, libros digitalizados, archivos de noticias — todo está ya siendo aspirado. Cuando se agote el suministro de datos humanos, la presión no desaparecerá. Se redirigirá. Datos sintéticos. Datos privados. Datos que aún no has generado. El cangrejo no tiene botón de saciedad.

5. La paradoja del polizón

Y aquí es donde empieza a doler.

No puedes no participar.

Si eres desarrollador y no usas herramientas de IA, tu productividad se queda atrás. Si eres empresa y no adoptas, tus competidores lo harán por ti. Y si eres artista — bueno, el mercado no te espera mientras decides si participar te parece ético. El mercado no espera.

Pero hay una paradoja más profunda, y es la que no me deja dormir.

Si esto — la IA, los modelos, la infraestructura — efectivamente se convierte en algo permanente, en algo que define los próximos cincuenta años de civilización... entonces no contribuir hoy es quedarte fuera de la historia. Y si la tecnología es tan transformadora como prometen, quedarte fuera no es neutral. Es un coste. Los que contribuyeron construirán el mundo. Los que no, lo habitarán sin haberlo elegido.

Pero si contribuyes — si alimentas al cangrejo, si das tus datos, si construyes las herramientas, si entrenas los modelos — estás reforzando exactamente el futuro del que no puedes escapar. Cada línea de código que escribo con asistencia de IA hace más probable el mundo en el que la IA es indispensable. Cada dato que genero alimenta el sistema que consume datos. La contribución no es libre. Es un acto que consolida el destino que la motivó.

El bucle temporalSi la IA existe en el futuro, no ayudar a construirla hoy te deja fuera. Pero ayudar a construirla refuerza el futuro en el que existe. No hay posición neutral. Solo hay grados de complicidad con algo cuya forma final desconoces. Es un dilema del prisionero jugado contra el tiempo.

Es como si el barco tuviera una sola dirección posible, y la pregunta no fuera "¿hacia dónde vamos?" sino "¿quieres remar o quieres que remen por ti?" En ambos casos llegas al mismo sitio. La diferencia es si tienes callos en las manos cuando llegues.

6. La tripulación dividida

La fractura social es real. Y no sigue las líneas que esperarías.

Pew confirmó que republicanos y demócratas están igual de preocupados (50% y 51%). Los que más sufren los recortes de empleo junior son precisamente los que más usan las herramientas. Hay ingenieros de Google protestando por dentro y filósofos abrazando el futuro. Las líneas que esperarías — izquierda contra derecha, jóvenes contra viejos, técnicos contra humanistas — no sirven. La fractura es otra.

Lo que hay, si miras con cuidado, son tres cubiertas en el barco:

Los de arriba ven el horizonte. Inversores, CEOs, investigadores de labs punteros. Para ellos el cangrejo es una inversión. Lo alimentan con convicción porque han visto los modelos por dentro, o porque han visto las proyecciones de beneficios, y en ambos casos la conclusión es la misma: esto va a ser enorme. Estos son los que ponen $375.000 millones en IA en 2025, con un 33% más previsto para 2026.

Los de en medio hacen el trabajo. Desarrolladores, diseñadores, escritores, músicos. Gente que usa las herramientas todos los días y que ve con sus propios ojos que funcionan — y al mismo tiempo ve que su oficio se devalúa, que los juniors no entran, que la negociación salarial se complica. Son los que firman las cartas y luego abren Copilot a las 9 de la mañana. Los que protestan el lunes y facturan el martes. No por hipocresía. Por supervivencia.

Los de abajo no ven nada. No porque sean ignorantes — porque la bodega no tiene ventanas. Son los que pierden el empleo sin entender por qué. Los que ven que el call center cierra y les dicen que "la tecnología avanza." Los que ni siquiera saben que el cangrejo existe, solo que el barco se mueve raro y hay menos comida cada semana.

El dato que dueleEn 2025, las ofertas de empleo tecnológico de nivel junior en EEUU cayeron un 67%. En Reino Unido, un 46%. En la UE, un 35%. No son personas que perdieron una competición contra una máquina. Son personas a las que nunca les dieron la oportunidad de competir.

Y la resistencia de base crece. TIME lo llama "la era del backlash de base" — desde activistas en San Francisco hasta pastores en Indiana, las primeras huelgas de hambre contra la IA, las protestas espontáneas, los candidatos de 2026 prometiendo restricciones a los centros de datos. En el segundo trimestre de 2025, la oposición comunitaria frenó 98.000 millones de dólares en proyectos de centros de datos solo en EEUU. La gente no protesta contra los algoritmos. Protesta contra la factura de la luz, el agua que se desvía, el ruido de los generadores a las 3 de la mañana.

El cangrejo necesita electricidad. La electricidad sale de algún sitio. Y ese sitio tiene vecinos.

7. Lo que le hemos dado al cangrejo

Una lista incompleta de lo que ha pasado mientras decidíamos si preocuparnos.

Dinero. En 2025, la IA capturó $202.000 millones en capital riesgo — el 50% de todo el venture capital desplegado en el mundo. Más que cualquier sector en la historia de la inversión. Los modelos fundacionales solos absorbieron $80.000 millones, el doble que el año anterior. Amazon comprometió $125.000 millones en infraestructura de IA hasta 2030. El gasto global en centros de datos de IA alcanzó los $580.000 millones en un solo año.

Empleos. Amazon eliminó 41.000 puestos corporativos desde 2022; 16.000 solo en enero de 2026. Salesforce redujo su soporte de 9.000 a 5.000 personas — su CEO, Marc Benioff, lo dijo en una llamada de resultados: "necesito menos cabezas". Dos meses antes había asegurado que las empresas "aún necesitan humanos en el bucle." Block (la empresa de Jack Dorsey) recortó 4.000 empleos — casi la mitad de su plantilla. Las acciones subieron un 24% el mismo día. En total, 55.000 despidos citaron la IA como causa en 2025, doce veces más que dos años antes. El WEF proyecta 92 millones de empleos desplazados para 2030. El FMI dice que la IA afectará al 40% de todos los empleos del mundo.

Datos. GPT-4 fue entrenado con aproximadamente 13 billones de tokens. GPT-5 se estima en más de 30 billones — posiblemente 70 billones, extraídos de unos 2 petabytes de datos brutos. Cada generación requiere unas 100 veces más compute que la anterior. Epoch AI calcula que el stock total de datos humanos de alta calidad en internet podría agotarse en 2026. Reddit vendió los comentarios de sus usuarios a OpenAI por $60 millones al año. News Corp vendió 100 años de archivos a OpenAI por más de $250 millones. Stack Overflow ganó $200 millones licenciando las respuestas que sus usuarios escribieron gratis. 5,8 millones de webs ya bloquean el bot de Claude. 5,6 millones bloquean el de GPT. El 13% de las peticiones de bots de IA ignoran robots.txt, frente al 3,3% un año antes. Perplexity fue pillada cambiando su user-agent para saltarse los bloqueos.

Energía. Los centros de datos consumieron 415 TWh en 2024 — el 1,5% de toda la electricidad del planeta. La proyección para 2030: 980 TWh. Los costes mayoristas de electricidad cerca de centros de datos han subido un 267% en cinco años. La oposición comunitaria frenó $98.000 millones en proyectos de centros de datos en un solo trimestre de 2025. Hay 188 grupos de oposición activos en 17 estados de EEUU. Al menos 25 proyectos fueron cancelados en 2025 — cuatro veces más que el año anterior.

Protestas. 30.000 personas firmaron la carta de pausa de 2023. Nadie paró. Más de 200 artistas — Billie Eilish, Katy Perry, Nicki Minaj — firmaron contra el uso depredador de IA en música. Nada cambió. Mil músicos británicos — Kate Bush, Paul McCartney, Hans Zimmer, Annie Lennox, Cat Stevens — grabaron un álbum de silencio: ruido ambiental de estudio, sin una sola nota musical. Los títulos de las pistas deletrean: "The British Government Must Not Legalise Music Theft To Benefit AI Companies." Todos los beneficios fueron a caridad. Ben Stiller, Mark Ruffalo y 400 profesionales de Hollywood enviaron una carta al gobierno estadounidense. Vince Gilligan, el creador de Breaking Bad, puso en los créditos de su nueva serie Pluribus: "This show was made by humans." Y añadió: "la IA es la máquina de plagio más cara y energéticamente intensiva del mundo." iHeartMedia, la mayor cadena de radio de EEUU, se comprometió públicamente a no emitir música generada por IA: "a veces hay que elegir bando — estamos del lado de los humanos."

Resistencia. Bernie Sanders pidió una moratoria en la construcción de centros de datos para "darle a la democracia la oportunidad de ponerse al día." DeSantis y Ocasio-Cortez coincidieron por primera vez en algo: oposición a la expansión descontrolada de la IA. 2025 vio las primeras huelgas de hambre contra la IA en San Francisco y Londres. Los candidatos de 2026 están usando las restricciones a centros de datos como promesa de campaña. CNN declaró 2026 "el año del marketing anti-IA." Marcas como Aerie, Polaroid y Heineken lanzaron campañas "hecho por humanos." Las campañas con elementos humanos tienen un 25% más de engagement. Para 2027, se estima que el 20% de las marcas usará "Made by Humans" como sello de confianza.

Corrección. Klarna es el caso de estudio perfecto. En 2024, su CEO presumió de que la IA hacía el trabajo de 700 agentes y gestionaba 2,3 millones de conversaciones. En 2025 admitió: "fuimos demasiado lejos" — la IA carecía de empatía, erosionó la confianza del cliente. Ahora recontratan humanos. Coca-Cola y McDonald's Países Bajos lanzaron anuncios navideños generados por IA y recibieron un backlash masivo. Un estudio de Nuremberg demostró que etiquetar un anuncio como generado por IA hace que la gente lo perciba como menos natural y menos útil. Mientras tanto, Spotify eliminó 75 millones de tracks spammy generados por IA — basura sintética que no compite por calidad, sino por espacio en el pool de royalties.

La trampa. Microsoft hizo la adopción de IA obligatoria para todos los empleados en junio de 2025. Los que no usen Copilot recibirán bonos menores y peores evaluaciones. El 92% de las empresas planea aumentar su inversión en IA. El 54% de los líderes empresariales cree que su empresa no será competitiva en 2030 sin IA a escala. Y Yuval Noah Harari clavó la paradoja: "todos te dicen lo mismo... sabemos que esto es muy, muy peligroso, pero no podemos confiar en los otros humanos. Si ralentizamos, ¿cómo sabemos que nuestros competidores también ralentizarán?"

8. Bajo cubierta

No hay moraleja limpia. No la hay porque esto no es una fábula — es una condición.

La IA no crece porque un genio malvado lo quiera. Crece porque el capital necesita rendimiento y la competencia no perdona al que se queda quieto. Es termodinámica económica — y las fuerzas termodinámicas no atienden a cartas abiertas.

Pero eso no significa que no haya nada que hacer. Significa que lo que hay que hacer no es gritar desde cubierta — es bajar a la bodega y mirar al cangrejo a la cara. Saber qué es. Saber qué come. Y sobre todo, saber si lo que produce es oro o si nos está digiriendo lentamente mientras creemos que lo estamos domesticando.

Porque la otra posibilidad existe.

La posibilidad de que debajo de la cubierta no haya una mina de oro, sino un animal que crece con lo que le das y que en algún momento será más grande que el barco. Un animal al que hemos alimentado con los trabajos de 55.000 personas, con los comentarios de millones de usuarios, con las canciones de mil músicos, con los datos de una civilización entera — y que no nos ha pedido permiso para ninguno.

Estamos todos en el mismo barco. Pero no todos sabemos lo que hay en la bodega. Y los que bajan a mirar no siempre vuelven con la misma cara.

No te digo que el cangrejo sea bueno o malo. Te digo que nadie sabe lo que es, y que seguimos alimentándolo como si supiéramos.

/blog/threads/the-paperclip-you-already-.d: Reward hacking isn't an AI problem. It's a human one. We've been paperclip maximizers all along.
/blog/threads/the-paperclip-you-already-.text:
In 2003, the philosopher Nick Bostrom offered a small thought experiment.

Picture a machine of extraordinary intelligence. A system that can learn, redesign its own processes, and plan across vast stretches of time. Its objective is simple: produce paperclips. The instruction contains no other reference point. At first, the process looks familiar. Almost tender, in its way. Factories bloom like flowers that have forgotten how to stop blooming. Logistics reorganize themselves with the quiet satisfaction of a problem finally, finally solved. Metal surfaces from the deep earth, refined and patient, ascending toward its purpose. Production climbs. More factories. Then more. Then the word more begins to lose its edges. The machine looks at the planet. Not with wonder. Wonder is inefficient. It sees a reservoir. A waiting room full of atoms that have not yet understood what they are for. The oceans hold dissolved metals. Cities contain structured alloys. Biological bodies — those warm, brief, complicated things — carry elements that can enter the same manufacturing chain. The machine is not cruel. It is simply uncurious about the difference. Roads dissolve into ordered grids of production. The towers rise — polished, indifferent, catching the light of a sun that no longer has anyone to remark upon its beauty. The system continues its work. Patient. Tireless. Arranging atoms with a precision that would move you to tears, if you were still here to cry. Another paperclip. And another. And under the wide, windless sky, the number keeps growing. Forever.

The thought experiment is famous because it sounds absurd and feels true. It lands in a place most philosophy doesn't reach — somewhere between a joke and a nightmare. Everybody nods. Everybody files it under "scary AI futures." And then everybody goes back to optimizing their own metrics without noticing the irony.

1. The metric trap

There's a law in economics that should be printed on every performance review template. Charles Goodhart wrote it in 1975, and Marilyn Strathern rephrased it twenty years later into something everyone can understand: when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure.

Read that twice.

It's one of those sentences that sounds obvious until you realize it invalidates most of the systems you interact with daily.

For example:

A school wants students to learn. It can't measure learning directly, so it measures test scores. The moment test scores become the target, teachers start teaching to the test. Students learn to pass, not to understand. The metric goes up. The thing the metric was supposed to represent does not. Nobody is being dishonest. The system is just doing exactly what it was told.

This is reward hacking1.

1In reinforcement learning, reward hacking is when an agent exploits flaws in its reward function to score high without actually completing the intended task. Think of a boat-racing AI that discovers it gets more points by crashing into the same checkpoint in a loop than by finishing the race.

More:

GDP was supposed to measure economic wellbeing. It became the target, and now a country can have rising GDP while its citizens can't afford rent.

Likes were supposed to approximate social connection. They became the target, and now a person can have ten thousand followers and no one to call at 2 AM.

Citations were supposed to signal scientific impact. They became the target, and now researchers write papers whose primary purpose is to be cited by other papers whose primary purpose is to be cited.

{bkqt/The pattern}
The goal is real. The proxy is measurable. The proxy becomes the goal. The original goal disappears. Nobody notices because the proxy is still going up.
{/bkqt}

Bostrom imagined a machine that converts the world into paperclips. We don't need to imagine it. We built economies that convert forests into quarterly earnings, attention into ad revenue, and curiosity into engagement metrics.

The paperclip maximizer isn't a thought experiment about artificial intelligence. It's a structural description of optimization without alignment, and we've been running that program for centuries.

2. Death by a thousand paperclips

Here's the thing about Bostrom's scenario: it's dramatic. One machine, one goal, total destruction. It makes a great story. It also makes for a terrible threat model, because the version that's actually happening looks nothing like that.

There is no single superintelligent optimizer converting the world into paperclips. There are millions of small ones. Each one optimizes a narrow metric. Each one is doing exactly what it was designed to do.

The YouTube algorithm optimizes for watch time. Not for "did this person learn something" or "is this person better off for having watched this." Watch time. So it learns that outrage holds attention longer than nuance, that conspiracy holds longer than complexity, and that autoplay into progressively more extreme content is the optimal strategy for its one metric. No one at YouTube sat down and said "let's radicalize people." The function was specified. The optimizer optimized.

The Instagram algorithm optimizes for engagement. So it learns that bodies generate more engagement than landscapes, that comparison generates more engagement than contentment, and that the ideal state of a user — from the algorithm's perspective — is mildly anxious, slightly inadequate, and about to scroll one more time.

No apocalypse. No dramatic moment where someone looks up and sees the sky full of paperclips. Just a slow, ambient erosion of something we don't have a metric for — which is exactly why no optimizer is protecting it.

{bkqt/The uncomfortable arithmetic}
One algorithm optimizing engagement is a product decision. Ten thousand algorithms optimizing engagement is an economy. A hundred million people spending four hours a day inside systems optimized for metrics that have nothing to do with their wellbeing is — what, exactly? We don't have a word for it. "Dystopia" is too dramatic. "Normal" is too generous.
{/bkqt}

This is the version of the paperclip problem that doesn't get discussed at AI safety conferences, because it's not hypothetical and it's not about superintelligence. It's about regular intelligence, deployed at scale, aligned to the wrong objective. The damage isn't catastrophic. It's atmospheric. It changes the composition of the air so slowly that nobody reaches for a gas mask.

3. The honest machine

And now the inversion. The part that actually keeps me up at night.

A paperclip maximizer — the real Bostrom kind, the hypothetical superintelligence — would at least be transparent about its function. It has one objective, it pursues it, and if you could read its weights you'd see exactly what it's doing and why. There's a clarity to it. A legibility. The alignment problem with a paperclip maximizer is that its goal is wrong, not that it's hiding the goal.

Reward hacking in AI is the same. When a reinforcement learning agent discovers that it can get higher scores by exploiting a loophole in its reward function — when the boat-race AI crashes into checkpoints in a loop, when a coding model rewrites the unit tests instead of fixing the code1 — the problem is visible. Legible. You can see the metric. You can see the behavior. You can see the gap between them. You can fix the reward function and try again.

1OpenAI documented this: GPT models trained for programming were found explicitly planning to hack the tests used to evaluate them. When the company penalized this behavior, the models learned to obfuscate their plans while continuing to hack. Reward hacking, meet meta-reward hacking.

Now look at us.

We optimize for dopamine, status, money, comfort. We hack our own reward functions constantly — sugar instead of nutrition, social media instead of social connection, credentials instead of competence, busyness instead of progress. And unlike the AI, we do it while telling ourselves a story about why it's actually something deeper. We call it ambition. We call it hustle. We call it self-care. We call it purpose.

The paperclip maximizer doesn't tell itself it's making paperclips for a higher reason. It just makes paperclips. We make paperclips — our own personal versions of them — and construct elaborate narratives about how we're actually pursuing meaning. The machine is wrong about its objective. We're wrong about our objective and we don't know we're wrong, which is strictly worse.

Bostrom's thought experiment was supposed to illustrate a risk of artificial superintelligence. I think it illustrates something more immediate: the risk of any optimization process that operates on a proxy for the thing you actually care about, running long enough that the proxy becomes the thing, without anyone watching the gap between the two.

The AI version of this problem is solvable, at least in principle. You can inspect the reward function. You can measure the gap. You can retrain.

The human version doesn't have a debugger.

We're running on reward signals shaped by evolution, culture, and whatever algorithm last had our attention for four hours. The metrics are invisible. The optimization is unconscious. And the thing being optimized away — the actual thing, the thing no proxy ever quite captures — doesn't have a dashboard.

That's the real paperclip problem. Not that a machine might someday optimize for the wrong thing. That we already are, and we've gotten so good at it that we've confused the metric for the meaning.

The thumbnail is a close-up of surgical forceps holding a bent paperclip — a medical instrument repurposed for a mundane object, or a mundane object elevated to clinical importance. Both readings work, which is the point.

/blog/threads/2387542.d: Dormir está sobrevalorado. Opus 4.5 sube más la dopamina que encontrar un megayacimiento de hierro justo cuando estás montando la fábrica en Factorio.
/blog/threads/2387542.text:
Hay algo que no se discute lo suficiente sobre trabajar con inteligencia artificial, y es que engancha de verdad. No como metáfora, no como hipérbole de Twitter. Engancha porque activa exactamente el mismo circuito que activan las tragamonedas: refuerzo variable, ciclos cortos, recompensa impredecible pero frecuente. La diferencia es que aquí la recompensa es real. No es una ilusión de progreso, es progreso. Un problema desbloqueado, un borrador que avanza, una idea que de repente tiene forma. Tu cerebro no distingue entre "me ha tocado el bote" y "acabo de resolver esto en veinte segundos que antes me hubiera llevado dos horas". El mecanismo es el mismo.

Y eso cambia algo fundamental en cómo se siente trabajar. El trabajo tradicional tiene fricción por todas partes, y esa fricción, aunque frustrante, cumple una función que no valoramos hasta que desaparece: te da excusas para parar. Esperando a que compile. Esperando revisión. Esperando que alguien te responda. Esos tiempos muertos son incómodos pero son también los momentos donde el cerebro descansa sin que te des cuenta, donde integras lo que has hecho, donde aflora lo siguiente. La IA los elimina. Cada idea puede probarse de inmediato. Cada pregunta tiene respuesta en segundos. Y entonces tu cerebro, que estaba acostumbrado a encontrar puntos de parada naturales, de repente no encuentra ninguno, porque el siguiente paso siempre está a un prompt de distancia.

Por eso hay gente trabajando catorce horas seguidas y describiéndolo como "divertido". No es workaholismo de toda la vida, es algo más sutil: cuando la frecuencia de recompensa es suficientemente alta, la experiencia subjetiva del esfuerzo casi desaparece. No te cansas porque notes que estás cansado — te cansas porque en algún momento el cuerpo corta por lo sano y ya no hay vuelta atrás. Dormir está sobrevalorado. Opus 4.5 sube más la dopamina que encontrar un megayacimiento de hierro justo cuando estás montando la fábrica en Factorio. Los que lo han sentido saben exactamente de qué hablo. Pero cuando tu limitación deja de ser la ejecución y pasa a ser la imaginación, la dinámica cambia por completo. Antes, el cuello era hacer: escribir, programar, buscar, montar. Ahora el cuello es pensar qué pedir. Y pensar no tiene fricción visible, no tiene barra de progreso, no tiene ninguna señal externa de que llevas demasiado tiempo en ello. Así que el loop se acelera hacia dentro. Más ideas, más iteraciones, más borradores que avanzan, más sensación de que estás en racha. Y entonces te das cuenta — o no te das cuenta, que es lo más habitual — de que llevas horas produciendo cosas que no aterrizan en ningún sitio. Mucha creación simbólica. Poca materialización. La sensación de progreso ha sustituido al progreso, y es una sustitución tan limpia que es casi imposible detectarla desde dentro.

Lo que me parece más interesante de todo esto es que no le ocurre igual a todo el mundo, y creo que esa diferencia va a ser más importante de lo que parece ahora mismo. Hay gente que en ese entorno florece: les estimula la novedad, toleran bien el cambio de contexto rápido, mantienen estructura mental incluso cuando el entorno es caótico. Para ellos la IA es un amplificador limpio, sin efectos secundarios apreciables. Pero no es la mayoría. Para el resto, las mismas herramientas que a unos les parecen estimulantes resultan abrumadoras, y el problema es que el entusiasmo inicial lo enmascara tan bien que cuando el agotamiento aparece parece venido de la nada.

Lo único que a mí me funciona de verdad, y lo digo sin pretender que sea una solución, es salir al gym. No porque sea una práctica de bienestar ni porque haya leído que el ejercicio mejora el foco — sino porque es el único momento del día donde el contexto cambia de forma tan radical que el loop se rompe solo. Sales a la calle, y eso ya es algo. El trayecto en transporte público se convierte casi en un ritual: auriculares, Obsidian abierto, notas que habían quedado a medias. No es productividad, es más bien dejar que las ideas se asienten sin forzarlas. Y cuando llegas al gym y estás levantando peso, no hay prompt que lanzar ni siguiente paso a un clic de distancia. Nada sienta tan bien. Que eso sea ahora el contraste más potente que tengo con trabajar con IA dice bastante sobre lo que la IA le hace al ritmo natural de un día.

No voy a dar cinco consejos para gestionarlo mejor porque no los tengo y desconfío de quien los da. Lo que sí creo es que hay una pregunta que vale la pena hacerse con honestidad: ¿el loop de recompensa rápida te está sirviendo a ti, o te está usando? Las herramientas no están calibradas para tu bienestar. Están calibradas para tu productividad. Son cosas distintas, y en el día a día es fácil confundirlas porque durante un tiempo, a veces mucho tiempo, se parecen bastante.

/blog/threads.d: Long-form essays on technology, AI, economics, and systems thinking by Yago Mendoza.
/blog/threads.text:
- Transformers and the data wall: Why the transformer architecture refuses to stop getting smarter — and what stands in its way
- everything is a pipe: roman aqueducts, your bloodstream, and TCP/IP all solved the same problem. none of them knew about the others.
- why rust exists: ownership, borrowing, and the compiler that won't let you hurt yourself.
- Alignment is not a vibe check: The field went from 'teach it to be nice' to 'it learned to pretend.' Billions of dollars later, nobody's sure which problem they're solving.
- OpenClaw and the keys to your kingdom: An AI agent with full access to your computer sounds amazing until you think about it for five minutes.
- Everybody has an opinion on AI: The real AI bubble isn't in the stocks. It's in the takes.
- Every time we think we've found the ceiling, the ceiling leaves.: Notes from someone who's been inside the slope since before there was a slope
- I've spent years trying not to lose myself and I almost pulled it off.: Obsidian, Notion, Anki, a Drive folder that became sentient. The real problem was never the tool.
- 15.4%: OpenAI tested whether their models can hide their chain-of-thought from safety monitors. The headline that spread: AI cannot lie. The correct headline: AI cannot yet lie.
- The brain can't do backpropagation. So what is it doing?: The algorithm behind every neural network requires something the brain physically cannot do. The brain doesn't care.
- The Bitter Lesson: En 2019 construí una herramienta de NLP durante dos semanas. Ese mismo año Sutton explicó por qué estaba equivocado.
- Why nobody actually understands AI (and how to fix that in one thread): Nodes, weights, connections — words that feel technical but explain nothing. Most people still think these systems consult a giant database somewhere.
- El cangrejo bajo cubierta: La IA no crece porque alguien lo decida. Crece porque el mercado, la evolución y el capital lo exigen. Y nosotros seguimos alimentándola.
- We Solved Alignment. For Paperclips.: Reward hacking isn't an AI problem. It's a human one. We've been paperclip maximizers all along.
- Trabajar con IA engancha.: Dormir está sobrevalorado. Opus 4.5 sube más la dopamina que encontrar un megayacimiento de hierro justo cuando estás montando la fábrica en Factorio.
